client: I've been really struggling since last week when our team missed a major project deadline. I'm new to this project manager role and I feel like everything just fell apart on my watch, and now I can't stop replaying all the things I should have done differently. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to fix anything, because the damage is already done.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy weight right now — the self-blame, the replaying of events, and on top of that, a sense of hopelessness that even talking won't help. That last part stands out to me, because sometimes when we're in the thick of that kind of pain, it can feel like nothing will move it — but I'm curious, what would it mean for you if talking *did* help, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I guess if talking actually helped, it would mean... I don't know, maybe that I'm not as stuck as I feel? But honestly, part of me is scared to hope for that, because I've tried talking before and I just end up going in circles, rehashing the same stuff without anything actually changing. It's like, what's the point of understanding why I feel guilty about how things ended with my dad if I can't go back and fix it?
therapist: There's something really tender in what you just shared — you moved from the work deadline all the way to your dad, and I don't think that was accidental. It sounds like underneath the guilt about the project, there might be a much older, deeper pain about things feeling unfinished or unfixable. I'm wondering, when you imagine being "stuck," does it sometimes feel like it's bigger than just this one missed deadline?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah... I think you're right that it wasn't accidental. When I said "stuck," something in my chest just kind of tightened, because it does feel bigger — like this pattern has been following me around for years, not just with this deadline but with a lot of things I've left unfinished or avoided. And my dad... we never really resolved anything before he passed, and I think part of me wonders if I'm just wired to leave things incomplete, like it's just who I am.
therapist: What you just said — "I'm just wired to leave things incomplete, like it's who I am" — that's a really significant belief to carry, and I want to gently pause there, because that sounds less like a fact about you and more like a story that's been building for a long time, maybe reinforced by a lot of pain. I also noticed you spoke quite quickly just now, like there's a lot rushing through you at once — I'm wondering if part of you has been waiting a long time to say all of this out loud. What feels most true to you: that you *are* someone who leaves things unfinished, or that you've been carrying an enormous amount of loss that made finishing feel impossible?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean... when you put it that way, it catches me off guard a little, because I've been telling myself the first version for so long that it just feels like fact. But yeah, I did rush through all of that, and I think it's because some part of me was scared if I slowed down I'd lose my nerve or start crying. I want to say the second thing feels more true, but honestly it's hard to fully believe it yet, because the evidence of all the unfinished things is just... right there, staring at me.
therapist: The fact that you *want* to believe the second version, even if you can't fully yet — that's not nothing, that's actually really important. And what you said about slowing down and losing your nerve tells me there's real courage in what you're doing right now, even if it doesn't feel that way. I'm curious — when you look at those "unfinished things," is there any part of you that can see how some of them might have been less about who you are, and more about circumstances that were simply too painful or too big to face alone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... yeah, maybe. There are a few things I left behind that I think, if I'm honest, I just didn't have anyone in my corner at the time. But it's hard not to feel like that's just an excuse, like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily by blaming circumstances instead of just admitting I gave up.
therapist: There's a really important distinction hiding in what you just said — an "excuse" is something we use to avoid accountability, but what you're describing sounds more like *context*, and context isn't the same as letting yourself off the hook. I also notice you said it quite softly, almost carefully, like you're testing whether it's okay to be even a little bit kind to yourself. What do you think it would mean about you as a person if it turned out that needing support wasn't a weakness, but just... a human thing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but there's this other part that immediately goes, "yeah, but that's just something people say to make you feel better." Like, in my family growing up, needing help was genuinely seen as a burden, so it's hard to just flip that switch and decide it's okay now. If needing support is just a human thing, I guess that would mean I've been punishing myself for something that was never actually a flaw, and honestly that thought makes me feel kind of... sad? Like, that's a lot of years of being hard on myself for no real reason.
therapist: That sadness you're naming makes complete sense — there's a kind of grief in realizing you've been carrying a rule about yourself that was never really yours to begin with, it was handed to you by people who were probably just passing on their own pain. And even as you said something so tender and significant, I noticed you moved through it quite quickly, like maybe part of you is still a little uncomfortable letting that realization fully land. What would it feel like to just sit with that sadness for a moment, instead of moving past it — do you think it deserves a little space?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess I did move past it pretty fast, didn't I. It's just... sitting with sadness feels kind of pointless to me, like what does it actually do except make you feel worse? But I can feel something tightening in my chest right now even just thinking about slowing down and staying with it, so maybe you're onto something.
therapist: That tightening in your chest is actually really important information — your body is telling you something that the part of your mind calling sadness "pointless" is trying to talk you out of. Sitting with sadness isn't about making yourself feel worse; in CBT we'd say it's about letting an emotion complete its natural cycle instead of keeping it frozen in place by always moving away from it. I'm wondering — what do you think that tightness might be protecting you from, if you did let yourself slow down and stay with it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess... if I'm honest, the tightness is probably protecting me from feeling just how alone I actually am. Like if I slow down and really sit with it, I'm scared I'll realize that the loneliness isn't just a temporary thing — that it's something deeper and maybe harder to fix. That feels really overwhelming to even say out loud.
therapist: What you just said took real courage — naming the fear that the loneliness might be deep and lasting, that's one of the hardest things to say out loud. And yet even as you said something so vulnerable and heavy, there was something almost gentle in your voice, like a part of you feels a quiet relief at finally letting that truth surface. I'm wondering if, alongside the fear, there's also something that feels like release in not having to keep that hidden anymore?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, slow speech

client: I guess... yeah, maybe there is something like that. Like I've been carrying this weight of pretending everything is fine, telling people "oh I'm just busy" when really I just haven't had a real conversation with anyone in weeks. Saying it out loud here does feel different, but I'm also a little scared that the relief is temporary, like it'll just settle back into the same heaviness once I leave this room.
therapist: The fear that the relief won't last is so understandable, especially when you've been carrying this alone for so long — but I want to gently offer that what just happened here isn't nothing, because you named something real and true, and that doesn't un-happen when you leave. In CBT, we'd say that moments like this one are actually evidence you can begin to collect — proof that connection and relief are possible for you, even if they've felt out of reach. What might it look like to hold onto that, even just a little, as a small piece of evidence against the story that the loneliness is permanent?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to hold onto it, I really do. But I guess I'm scared that this feels different here, in this room, with you, because it's kind of your job to listen and not judge me, you know? Like, out there, with actual people in my life, I don't think it would go the same way, so I'm not sure it counts as the same kind of evidence.
therapist: That's a really honest and important pushback, and I don't want to dismiss it — you're right that this space is different, and it makes sense to wonder if it "counts." But I'm curious about something: the way you said all of that was quite soft, almost careful, like there's a part of you that *wants* to be wrong about this — like you're hoping I might offer something that helps the evidence feel more real. What would need to be true about the people in your life for connection with them to feel even a little bit safer to try?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
